findings.statement: The information customers enter into the chatbot, such as their name, account number and address, is personal data relating to identified or identifiable natural persons, and the chatbot processes it by automated means, so the GDPR applies to the company's operation of the chatbot.

The company's processing of customer data through the chatbot is lawful only if based on one of the Article 6(1) grounds, such as the customer's consent or the necessity of the processing for performing the customer-service contract, and it must settle on that ground for the chatbot's stated purposes.

Because customers type the data in directly, the company must provide them, at the time of collection, with the Article 13(1) information: the company's identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis of the chatbot processing, the recipients or categories of recipients, the data subjects' access, rectification, erasure, restriction and objection rights, the right to withdraw consent where consent is the legal basis, and the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority.

The name, account number and address the chatbot collects must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for answering the customer-service questions put to it, so its input fields and prompt handling may not sweep in data the query does not require.

The company must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, taking into account the state of the art and the risks of the processing, to secure the personal data entered into and generated by the chatbot, including against accidental destruction, loss or unauthorised disclosure of or access to the data.

If the model provider processes customers' personal data on the company's behalf, for example where the chatbot calls a hosted model service rather than running a self-hosted model, the provider is a processor, the company may use only processors providing sufficient guarantees, and the arrangement must be governed by a contract containing the Article 28(3) terms.

The chatbot, which only answers customer-service questions and cannot make changes to customer accounts, involves no decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects customers, so the right protected by Article 22(1) is not engaged by its operation.

A personal data breach affecting the information customers enter into the chatbot must be notified to the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the company becomes aware of it, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

The company uses the chatbot under its authority for a professional customer-service activity, which makes it the chatbot's deployer under Article 3(4), and as a deployer it must take measures, to its best extent, to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of its staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of the chatbot on its behalf.

Customers must be informed that they are interacting with an AI system: Article 50(1) requires the chatbot's provider to design it so that the natural persons concerned are told this unless it is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and the company owes that duty where it developed or had developed the chatbot and put it into service under its own name or trademark as provider under Article 3(3).

Answering customer-service questions about accounts is none of the Annex III areas, which run from biometrics and critical infrastructure through eligibility evaluation, creditworthiness scoring, insurance pricing, emergency-call handling, law enforcement, migration and justice, so the chatbot is not classified high-risk under Article 6(2) and the high-risk deployer obligations do not attach to the company.

The external model provider, as provider of the general-purpose AI model powering the chatbot, must draw up and keep up-to-date the model's technical documentation set out in Annex XI, make available to the chatbot's integrator documentation enabling a good understanding of the model's capabilities and limitations, put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright, and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training the model.

DORA does not apply to the company's operation of the chatbot: a telecommunications operator serving its own customers is not one of the entities listed in Article 2(1), and DORA's requirements for ICT third-party service providers arise only from contractual arrangements with financial entities, of which the scenario contains none.

summaries.relevance: Establishes that the chatbot's automated handling of customer data brings the company within the GDPR, which carries every controller duty the findings describe.
Definition that fixes the name, account number and address customers submit as personal data, the anchor for the GDPR's application.
Operative cap on the chatbot's input fields, requiring the data gathered per conversation to be limited to what the query needs.
Gateway duty on which all chatbot processing of customer data rests: the company must have a lawful ground such as consent or contract performance.
Defines the collection-time disclosure the company owes customers who type personal data into the chatbot, the main customer-facing compliance surface.
Delimits automated decision-making, letting the answer rule the read-only chatbot out of its safeguards.
Covers the processor contract owed to the model provider if it processes customer data on the company's behalf.
Sets the security duty protecting the personal data flowing into and out of the chatbot.
Fixes the 72-hour breach-notification duty that reaches incidents affecting chatbot data.
Definition that classes the company as the chatbot's deployer, the role carrying its AI Act duties.
Definition of provider whose Article 50(1) duty reaches the company if it built the chatbot under its own name or trademark.
The only direct AI Act operating duty on the company here, requiring staff AI literacy for the chatbot's use.
With Annex III, classifies the chatbot outside the high-risk regime, confining the company's AI Act duties to transparency and literacy.
Its exhaustive use-case list contains no customer-service chatbot, which is what keeps the system out of the high-risk classification.
Creates the signature requirement of this scenario, informing customers they are interacting with an AI system, and allocates it to the chatbot's provider.
Loads the model provider with the GPAI duties, from technical documentation to the training-content summary, that the company should confirm through its licence.
Frames DORA's requirements around the business processes of financial entities and their ICT contracts with third-party providers, none of which the scenario involves.
Its closed enumeration of in-scope entities contains no telecommunications operator, ruling the company out of DORA.

actions: Verify the company's and its customers' establishment or location in the Union, on which GDPR Article 3 territorial scope and AI Act Article 2(1) applicability to the deployment turn.

Settle how the licensed model is accessed, company-hosted versus provider-hosted, since that decides whether the model provider is a GDPR processor requiring an Article 28(3) contract and whether Chapter V transfer safeguards would apply if the provider processes the data outside the Union.

Establish who developed the chatbot and under whose name it is put into service, to determine whether the company is the chatbot's provider under AI Act Article 3(3) and thus owes the Article 50(1) AI-interaction notice.
Assess against the actual website design whether interacting with an AI is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect customer, which could disapply the Article 50(1) notice.

Determine whether the chatbot's processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of customers, which would require a data protection impact assessment under GDPR Article 35(1) before deployment.
